description: ELUNARA is a team of curious minds passionate about space, science and technology. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we explore Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and satellite data, turning complex observations into meaningful insights. With creativity, teamwork and innovation, we aim to discover new perspectives of our planet and think beyond the ordinary.
summary:
Slopewise turns a NISAR L-band interferogram into a review map for slope movement near Joshimath, Uttarakhand. It shows observed line-of-sight deformation, the noise floor of the scene, and a grey blind-zone mask marking where the radar cannot give a reliable measurement. In steep, forested and snowy terrain most pixels are unusable, and a tool that hides this would mislead.

Using one provisional pair (26 September to 20 October 2026), Slopewise finds two candidate hotspots that exceed the noise floor of about 26 mm. It adds terrain slope and downslope flow paths from a 30 m elevation model, and the nearest roads and settlements from OpenStreetMap. Each hotspot gets a relative review-priority score and a downloadable evidence report listing its limitations.

Slopewise reports observed deformation and exposure. It does not predict landslides. The data is provisional, covers a single 12-day pair, has 80 m pixels, and has no retrospective validation. The hotspots are candidates for field inspection, not confirmed movement. Next steps are validated pairs as the archive grows and a check against field or other InSAR data.
details:
What it does and how it works

Slopewise turns a NISAR L-band GUNW interferogram into a review map of slope movement near Joshimath, Uttarakhand. It reads the unwrapped phase, converts it to line-of-sight displacement, removes a planar ramp, and masks low-coherence pixels (threshold 0.3). It then estimates the scene’s noise floor (about 26 mm) and keeps only clusters of movement that exceed it. The grey blind-zone mask shows where the radar cannot give a reliable measurement, and the app states that grey does not mean stable. Terrain slope and downslope flow paths come from the Copernicus 30 m DEM. Nearby roads and settlements come from OpenStreetMap (146 roads and 89 places in the area). Each hotspot gets a relative review-priority score and a downloadable evidence report that lists its limitations.

Benefits and intended impact

Many tools show deformation without saying where they cannot see. Slopewise shows what NISAR can and cannot measure, so planners and field teams can decide where to inspect first and where they need other data. In this run, only about 12% of pixels around Joshimath were usable, and the app shows that openly. The two candidate hotspots (+98.0 mm and +74.6 mm over about 6 ha) are leads for field inspection, not confirmed movement.

Tools used

Python (NumPy, rasterio , GeoPandas , Shapely, Matplotlib, requests), HDF5 reading for NISAR GUNW files, the Copernicus 30 m DEM, the OpenStreetMap Overpass API, QGIS for checking layers, and a Leaflet web app (HTML and JavaScript) with Esri satellite imagery as the base map. It runs on a normal laptop with no special hardware.

What is creative

The project is built around uncertainty. It shows the noise floor and the blind zone before any hotspot, keeps data maturity (provisional) visible, and reports exposure through downslope flow paths and nearby roads and settlements, not only straight-line buffers. Every hotspot ships with its own limitations.

Factors we considered

The data is provisional, and NASA documents a processing issue in provisional interferograms that can cause decorrelation. It is a single 12-day pair, so there is no time series and no trend. At 80 m pixels, only broad creep or large slides are visible. Line-of-sight motion is one-dimensional, and we have not verified the sign convention, so we do not claim direction. Atmospheric and ionospheric effects are only partly handled. The two priority scores are effectively tied (0.60 each), so we do not rank one hotspot above the other. The flow paths are a simple steepest-descent estimate, and the DEM includes vegetation and buildings. Rainfall was not evaluated. There is no retrospective validation, because NISAR launched in July 2025, after the 2024 Wayanad slide. Slopewise reports observed deformation and exposure. It does not predict landslides.
